claims.contract: TSDoc on the helper: "By default it also mirrors `aria-selected` onto the items (highlight doubles as selection, the command palette model); pass `ariaSelected: false` when items carry their own `aria-selected` for a stored value (e.g. a combobox), keeping the highlight a pure focus cue."
claims.evidence: use-a11y-roving.ts:92-103 — both `prev?.setAttribute('aria-selected','false')` and `next?.setAttribute('aria-selected','true')` sit inside `if (activeDescendantRef)`, so the `ariaSelected` option only has effect when an unrelated option is supplied. The indexed path does it right: `applyVirtualActiveDom` at :144-168 writes `aria-selected` outside any controller guard, and :218-224 documents `setVirtualActiveIndexed` as the "Indexed-source counterpart to {@link setVirtualActive}", i.e. same semantics. `moveTo` (:501-536) routes to whichever of the two applies, so the same widget can behave differently depending only on whether an item source is registered. Suspected severity: medium (a11y). Fix: lift the `ariaSelected` block out of the `activeDescendantRef` branch.

claims.trigger: Pass a status string that goes "3 results" → `null` (cleared while refetching) → "3 results"; equivalently, flip `enabled` false, let the message change, and flip it back.
claims.wrongResult: The returning value is never spoken, so a reader who changed the query and landed on the same count hears silence and cannot tell whether anything happened.
claims.contract: TSDoc: "Pass the current human-readable status (a result count, the active sort, the current page); it speaks whenever that string changes, skipping the initial value and consecutive duplicates."
claims.evidence: use-a11y-announcements.ts:32-40 — `if (!enabled) return` and `if (!message || message === previous.current) return` both return before `previous.current = message` at :37, so a falsy interlude (or a disabled window) freezes the baseline at the older value. The value that comes back is then compared against a baseline it is not consecutive with and is treated as a duplicate. Suspected severity: low-medium (a11y; silent status). Fix: write `previous.current = message ?? undefined` before the falsy bail and in the disabled branch, so the baseline always tracks the last value the reader could have heard.

claims.trigger: Pass an inline `transition` (or `ceilingOf`) object literal — neither option's TSDoc asks for a stable reference — and let the panel's owner re-render while a height travel is in flight.
claims.wrongResult: The effect tears down and rebuilds on that render: the in-flight travel is stopped and the inline pin is then cleared, so the panel snaps to its content height mid-animation; the observer's `rested` baseline also resets to null, so the next content change is adopted with no travel at all.
claims.contract: TSDoc `@param transition`: "The travel between two content heights. The panel's kata states it." — no stability requirement, against the package's own stated precedent in `useA11yRoving`: "Depend on the selector strings, not the `row` object: callers pass inline literals whose identity changes per render."
claims.evidence: use-panel-fit.ts:168 lists `[panel, enabled, dragged, ceilingOf, transition, reduced]` as effect deps; the cleanup at :159-167 runs `travel?.stop()` and `observer.disconnect()`, then the re-run clears the pin at :102 and re-declares `let rested: BorderBox | null = null` at :110. Compare use-a11y-roving.ts:870-874, which deliberately destructures the selector strings out of the `row` object for exactly this reason. Suspected severity: medium (visible animation break, and a silent loss of travel afterwards). Fix: shadow `transition`/`ceilingOf` in refs read inside the observer callback, or state the stability requirement on both options.

claims.trigger: Render with an explicit `width` (a fixed-width chart), then drop it to `undefined` to go responsive, without the observed container itself changing size.
claims.wrongResult: The hook keeps reporting width `0`, because the observed value was never taken while the explicit width was in force and nothing re-triggers a measurement; the colour range bar it positions collapses to the container's left edge until an unrelated resize happens.
claims.contract: TSDoc `@returns` on the `width` field: "The explicit width when one was given, else the observed one; `0` until the first measure." — and "An explicit `width` wins outright and never observes, so a fixed-width chart reads deterministically under SSR and in tests."
claims.evidence: use-measured-width.ts:43-55 — the `if (width !== undefined) return` bail sits inside the resize callback, while the subscription itself (use-resize-observer.ts:17-29) keys on `[ref]` alone and fires its one synchronous `onResize()` only when the effect first attaches. So when `width` clears, no path re-invokes the measurement and `measured` stays at its `useState(0)` seed (:37). Suspected severity: low (needs a width prop that toggles). Fix: re-measure when `width` transitions to `undefined`, e.g. an effect keyed on `width === undefined`.

claims.trigger: Pass an `onDismiss` closure that reads state which changes during the drag (a drawer whose close handler carries the current step or a pending selection), then flick the panel away to dismiss it.
claims.wrongResult: The dismissal runs the `onDismiss` captured at pointer-down, so the panel closes against the state the gesture began with rather than the state at release.
claims.contract: The rule the hooks layer states for caller callbacks, in `useDismissable`'s TSDoc: "Pass a fresh `onDismiss` closure each render if that is convenient; both routes reach the latest one, and neither re-subscribes its listener when the identity changes."
claims.evidence: use-panel-resize.ts:424-436 registers the render-scoped `release` (declared :343-376, closing over `onDismiss` from that render) on `window` under one AbortController; :412-414 then calls `setSize(measured)` and `setResizing(true)`, which re-render immediately, so every later render's `release` is unreachable for the rest of the gesture and only the pointer-down-render closure ever fires at :370. Every neighbouring hook shadows its caller callback instead (use-escape-layer.ts:40, use-dismissable.ts:51, use-resize-observer.ts:15, use-hover-across-scroll.ts:46-48). Suspected severity: low-medium. Fix: shadow `onDismiss` with `useEffectEvent`.

claims.trigger: Press an axis arrow key on the grab bar before the panel node has attached — the panel is portalled and mounts a commit after the bar, which is the case the hook's own node-as-state comment names.
claims.wrongResult: The keypress is consumed: nothing resizes and the page does not scroll either, so the arrow key is simply dead until the panel attaches.
claims.contract: TSDoc on the keyboard branch: "Never dismisses. The arrows resize, and Escape is how a panel closes from the keyboard everywhere else in the system" — the handler claims the key only for a resize it is able to perform.
claims.evidence: use-panel-resize.ts:439-444 — `event.preventDefault()` at :442 runs before the `if (panel === null) return` guard at :444; the hook itself documents at :252-254 that the panel "is portalled and mounts on a later commit than the one that opens the panel", so the null window is real rather than hypothetical. Suspected severity: low. Fix: move the null-panel guard above `preventDefault()`.

claims.trigger: Call it with a ref count that varies between renders — `useComposedRef(...refs)` over a list, or a ref omitted on some renders instead of passed as `undefined`.
claims.wrongResult: React reports that the memo's dependency array changed size between renders and the merged callback ref is rebuilt unpredictably, detaching and reattaching the node and nulling the composed refs in between.
claims.contract: The constraint the sibling states but the base hook does not: "Fixed arity, because these two reach the dependency array of the composed ref and React rejects an array whose length changes between renders."
claims.evidence: use-composed-ref.ts:15-17 forwards the rest array straight into floating-ui's `useMergeRefs`, which spreads it as the dependency list for both hooks it calls — packages/ui/node_modules/@floating-ui/react/dist/floating-ui.react.mjs:38 (`}, refs)` on the `useCallback`) and :53 (`}, refs)` on the `useMemo`). The quoted constraint lives at use-floating-reference.ts:33-35, i.e. the package already knows the rule but records it only on the derived helper, while `useComposedRef` is the barrel-public entry (hooks/index.ts:27). Suspected severity: low. Fix: state the fixed-arity requirement in the TSDoc, or normalise the array to a constant length before handing it over.

claims.trigger: Call `refocus(id)` after a keyboard reorder and unmount the list in the same frame — a drawer or popover that closes on drop.
claims.wrongResult: The queued frame still runs, so the caller's `focus` callback fires against a tree that is gone; and if the frame is dropped instead, `movingRef` is left true for the rest of the mount, so the next blur no longer clears the lifted item and it stays lifted forever.
claims.contract: TSDoc: "`refocus` restores focus on the frame after a reorder re-renders the DOM; blurs it causes keep the lifted state."
claims.evidence: use-keyboard-lifted.ts:22-33 — `requestAnimationFrame` is called with no handle stored and the hook registers no unmount cleanup, so nothing cancels a pending frame and nothing resets `movingRef` except the frame's own body at :29. The neighbouring frame-based hook does both: use-keyboard-settled.ts:68-75 holds the handle in a ref and cancels it in an unmount effect. Suspected severity: low. Fix: keep the handle in a ref, cancel it on unmount and on a superseding `refocus`, and reset `movingRef` there.

claims.trigger: Point it at an element inside a portalled surface that mounts a commit after `when` flips true — the presence-portal panel case the hook's own summary names as its use.
claims.wrongResult: `ref.current` is still null when the single effect runs, nothing re-runs it, and the panel opens with focus left where it was; only toggling `when` false and true again recovers it.
claims.contract: The rule the sibling states for this exact shape: "Observation must follow the node React attaches, and a portalled surface mounts its content a commit after the consumer renders — a `RefObject` reports that arrival to nothing, so the probe would read `null` once and never re-run." The hook itself promises: "Moves focus to `ref.current` whenever `when` flips true: initial focus for a panel that opens."
claims.evidence: use-a11y-auto-focus.ts:12-16 — the effect deps are `[when, ref]`, so a node attaching on a later commit produces no re-run and the `ref.current?.focus()` optional call silently no-ops. The quoted contract is use-a11y-has-tabbable.ts:14-18, which takes the node as state from a callback ref precisely to avoid this. Suspected severity: low-medium (a11y; keyboard focus stranded outside an opened panel). Fix: accept the node as state from a callback ref, or re-attempt on the commit after attachment.

leads.note: `accessibleName` reads `aria-labelledby` and passes the whole attribute value to `getElementById`. ARIA allows a space-separated id list, so `aria-labelledby="a b"` resolves to null and the function silently falls back to the element's own textContent, contradicting its stated "the trimmed text of its `aria-labelledby` target". Reached from use-typeahead.ts, where it decides which item a type-ahead keypress jumps to.

`announce` clears the live region then writes the message in a `queueMicrotask`. Two announcements in the same tick queue two microtasks against the same node, so the second overwrites the first before any observation and the first message is never spoken. Reached from use-a11y-announcements.ts.

`nextIndexForKey` handles Home/End before the grid branch, returning index 0 and `itemCount - 1` even when `cols` is set, so in a grid Home/End jump to the first/last cell of the whole grid rather than of the current row (APG grid pattern reserves Ctrl for the whole-grid move). Consumed by `useA11yRoving`'s `handleMainAxisNav`.

claims.trigger: Render `<DashboardLayout filters={<FilterPanel />}>…</DashboardLayout>` and view it at a viewport at or above the `lg` breakpoint.
claims.wrongResult: The desktop filter `aside` renders as a full-width block stacked above the main content column instead of sitting beside it; the rail's `shrink-0` and the main column's `min-w-0 flex-1` never take effect on the inline axis.
claims.contract: DashboardLayout TSDoc: "Wraps {@link StackedLayout} and, when `filters` is given, shows them beside the main column on desktop and inside an offcanvas drawer on mobile." The `filters` prop TSDoc: "Render inline as a desktop `aside`; on mobile they collapse behind a \"Filters\" button that opens them in a {@link Drawer}."
claims.evidence: dashboard.tsx:41 opens `<Stack gap="md">` with no `direction`. `Stack` (packages/ui/src/components/stack/stack.tsx:20) is `<Flex data-slot="stack" direction="col" {...props} />`, so the omitted prop leaves `direction="col"` → `flex-col`. Inside it, dashboard.tsx:45 renders `<aside … className="shrink-0 max-lg:hidden">` and dashboard.tsx:67 renders `<main data-slot="main" className="min-w-0 flex-1">`. `shrink-0` beside `min-w-0 flex-1` is the row idiom; in a column both siblings are full-width and the rail lands on top of the content. The mobile trigger (dashboard.tsx:50, `lg:hidden`) and the desktop aside (`max-lg:hidden`) are correctly breakpoint-gated, so the only broken axis is direction. Suspected severity: medium-high — a visible layout defect on every desktop render that passes `filters`. Fix idea: give the Stack a responsive direction (`direction={{ base: 'col', lg: 'row' }}`) or swap to `<Flex className="max-lg:flex-col lg:flex-row">`, matching the `max-lg:` / `lg:` gating already used on the two filter surfaces.

claims.trigger: Call `useCurrentState({ value: null, onValueChange })` — the §7.3 "controlled with no current value" form — feed the result into `CurrentContext`, and render two or more `<CurrentContent slotPrefix="tab" value="a" />` / `value="b"` panels inside a `<CurrentContents>`.
claims.wrongResult: Every panel renders as the current panel at once (each fade-mode panel is stamped `data-current` and positioned `relative`, none is `inert`) instead of no panel being current, so the surface shows all of its mutually exclusive views stacked together.
claims.contract: `useCurrentState` prop TSDoc: "Controlled active value. `undefined` leaves it uncontrolled; `null` keeps it controlled with none active (CONVENTIONS §7.3)." CONVENTIONS.md §7.3: "In value props, `undefined` leaves the control uncontrolled; `null` keeps it controlled with no current value."
claims.evidence: `CurrentContextValue.value` is typed `string | undefined` (current.ts:10), so the type has no representation for "controlled, none active". `useCurrentState` (current.ts:36-49) forwards `props.value` into `useControllable`, which normalises the clear to `undefined` — packages/ui/src/hooks/use-controllable.ts:34 `const currentValue = isControlled ? (value ?? undefined) : internalValue` and :55 `const normalized = resolved ?? undefined` ("Internally 'no value' is always `undefined`"). The memo at current.ts:48 then publishes `value: undefined`. `matchesCurrent` in packages/ui/src/primitives/current/current-content.tsx:63-65 returns `value === undefined || contextValue === undefined || contextValue === value`, so an `undefined` context value matches every panel — the documented "an unvalued context keeps every panel current" rule (current-content.tsx:57-58) now also swallows the explicit `null`. Downstream, current-content.tsx:99 `const current = matchesCurrent(...)` drives `data-current` (:146), `inert` (:171) and the `position: relative` branch (:167-169), and use-current-contents-morph.ts:154 sizes the container off every `data-current` child. Suspected severity: high — the §7.3 clear silently inverts into "show everything". Fix idea: widen `CurrentContextValue.value` to `string | null | undefined`, have `useCurrentState` pass a controlled `null` through unchanged, and make `matchesCurrent` return `false` when `contextValue === null` while keeping the `undefined` (unvalued) branch as it is.

claims.trigger: Inside a `<ToastProvider>`, call `toast({ title: 'A', duration: 10000 })`, then about one second later call `toast({ title: 'B', duration: 1000 })`.
claims.wrongResult: Toast A is removed roughly two seconds after it was raised, with `onDismiss('timeout')`, instead of living the ten seconds its own `duration` asked for; every non-persistent toast in the stack expires on whichever `duration` the most recent `toast()` call supplied.
claims.contract: `ToastProviderProps.duration` TSDoc: "Default lifetime (ms) for toasts that don't set `persist` or their own `duration`." `ToastInput` TSDoc (types.ts): "{@link ToastData} without the fields the provider derives", with `duration?: number` kept as a per-toast field, and `ToastDismissReason` TSDoc: "`timeout` is the toast's own lifetime running out".
claims.evidence: There is exactly one countdown for the whole stack: `useToastTimer` holds a single `timerRef` (use-toast-timer.ts:32) and one `remainingRef` (:30), and arms it with `setTimeout(start, remainingRef.current)` (:55). Every `toast()` call overwrites that shared countdown — toast.tsx:113 `resetRemaining(data.duration ?? duration)` then toast.tsx:115 `if (!data.persist) startTimer()`, and `startTimer` clears the pending timeout first (use-toast-timer.ts:51). When the single timer fires, `useToastQueue.start()` (use-toast-queue.ts:49-55) snapshots **every** non-persistent toast — `toastsRef.current.filter((t) => !t.persist).map((t) => t.id)` — and drains the whole list one exit-complete at a time (:57-59), so the per-toast `duration` stored at toast.tsx:102 is never read again after `resetRemaining`. `handleRemove` (toast.tsx:48-51) then reports `'timeout'` for each. `resetToast` (toast.tsx:124-133) writes the same shared value. Suspected severity: medium — a documented per-toast field is inert, and long-lived toasts vanish early whenever a short one follows. Fix idea: store an absolute `expiresAt` on each `ToastData` when it is enqueued, arm the timer for the nearest unexpired deadline, and have `start()` queue only the toasts whose deadline has passed.

claims.trigger: Import `useDensityLevel` from `ui/providers/density` into a React Server Component (a `page.tsx` or `layout.tsx` with no `'use client'`) and call it to resolve a `DensityLevel`.
claims.wrongResult: The render throws at runtime in the consuming Next app — the hook reaches a client-only export from the server graph — instead of returning the documented `'snug'` ambient fallback; nothing in the package surfaces the boundary at import time.
claims.contract: packages/ui/REFERENCE.md §2: "**Client components** keep `'use client'` in their own file (per [CONVENTIONS.md](../../CONVENTIONS.md) §2.2) and can read context freely." and "The static tier must not read the cascade (`useDensity` and friends)." `component-boundary.test.ts` states the same mechanism: "the package's subpath exports resolve to raw source, so a missing directive surfaces as an RSC crash only at runtime in a consuming Next app."
claims.evidence: providers/density/density.tsx carries no directive — line 1 is `import type { ReactNode } from 'react'`. It imports the cascade at line 2 (`import { Density as DensityPrimitive, useDensityNullable } from '../../primitives/density'`), and `useDensityLevel` (lines 47-51) calls `useDensityNullable()` at line 48; primitives/density/density.tsx line 1 is `'use client'`, so `useDensityNullable` is a client-only export. Every sibling provider that calls a hook does carry the directive: providers/glass/context.ts:1 (holds `useResolvedSurface`), providers/headless/context.ts:1, providers/locale/use-format.ts:1, providers/toast/context.ts:1, providers/toast/use-toast-timer.ts:1. The hook is public — providers/density/index.ts:2 re-exports it — and its own TSDoc scopes it to "a client component whose prop surface speaks `DensityLevel`", which the file never declares. `static-component-boundary.test.ts` walks only `src/components` plus a curated `STATIC_PRIMITIVE_FILES` list, so no gate covers this file. Suspected severity: medium. Fix idea: add `'use client'` to providers/density/density.tsx (the `DensityProvider` host stays server-composable because it is still just a wrapper), or split `useDensityLevel` into a directive-carrying `use-density-level.ts` and leave the provider directive-free.

claims.trigger: Pass a renaming anchor to the panel — `<CurrentContent slotPrefix="tab" value="a" data-slot="my-panel">…</CurrentContent>` — first inside a fading `<CurrentContents>` (the default) and then inside `<CurrentContents fade={false}>`.
claims.wrongResult: The rendered element carries `data-slot="my-panel"` under a non-fading container but keeps `data-slot="tab-content"` under a fading one, so the same markup yields two different query anchors and a `data-slot` test passes or fails depending only on the container's `fade` flag.
claims.contract: CONVENTIONS.md §3.9: "Presentational attributes stay overridable: a leaf's `data-slot` default is destructured so a consumer can rename the anchor, and `className` merges through `cn`." CONVENTIONS.md §10.2: "Component tests render through the library's test renderer and query by `data-slot`."
claims.evidence: The two render branches disagree on spread order. Non-fade branch: `data-slot={`${slotPrefix}-content`}` is written at line 128 and `{...props}` is spread last at line 131, so a caller's `data-slot` wins. Fade branch: `{...(props as HTMLMotionProps<'div'>)}` is spread first at line 144 and `data-slot={`${slotPrefix}-content`}` is re-written after it at line 145, so the primitive's value wins. `data-slot` is never destructured out of `props` (the destructure at lines 80-88 takes `slotPrefix`, `value`, `className`, `style`, `children`, `ref`), and TypeScript admits hyphenated JSX attributes on any component, so both paths type-check. Suspected severity: low — an inconsistent public anchor, not a functional break. Fix idea: destructure once at the top — `'data-slot': slot = `${slotPrefix}-content`` — and use `slot` in both branches, matching how `Box` (`'data-slot': slot = 'box'`) and `SelectTrigger` (`'data-slot': slot = 'control'`) already do it.

claims.trigger: Render a modal overlay with the backdrop turned off and the default dismissal flags — `<Overlay open onOpenChange={setOpen} backdrop={false}>…</Overlay>` — then press the pointer anywhere outside the panel.
claims.wrongResult: Nothing dismisses: the press is ignored even though `dismissOnBackdrop` is on by default, so the surface can only be closed with Escape or by the panel's own control. Turning off a purely visual flag silently removes a dismissal route.
claims.contract: The `backdrop` prop TSDoc frames it as a painting flag only — "Paint the dimming backdrop independently of modality. A non-modal surface (e.g. a hover-revealed sheet) can opt in to blur and dim the page while staying interactive". The `modal` prop TSDoc assigns outside-press dismissal to the non-modal arm — "Escape or a pointer press outside the panel dismisses" — and Overlay's own remark says "Manages focus trapping, body scroll lock, dismissal, and the dimming backdrop".
claims.evidence: `backdrop = modal` (line 113) so the flag defaults on for a modal surface, but it can be switched off independently. The two dismissal routes are mutually exclusive and both fail in that combination: `useDismissable` is wired with `outsidePointer: !modal && dismissOnBackdrop` (line 136) — false whenever `modal` is true — and the only other route is the backdrop's own `onClick={dismissOnBackdrop ? () => onOpenChange(false) : undefined}` (line 162), which sits inside the `{backdrop && (…)}` guard at line 153 and is therefore not rendered. The inline comment at lines 132-135 states the intended split ("Modal overlays own outside-press dismissal via the blocking backdrop's click handler") but never accounts for a modal overlay with no backdrop. `useEscapeLayer` inside `useDismissable` (packages/ui/src/hooks/use-dismissable.ts:53-57) still runs, which is why Escape survives. Suspected severity: low-medium. Fix idea: `outsidePointer: dismissOnBackdrop && (!modal || !backdrop)`, so the pointer route takes over whenever no backdrop is painted to own it.

claims.trigger: Render `<CurrentContents fade mount="active">` with two `CurrentContent` panels and one of them inactive, then re-render the same tree with `mount="always"` while that panel is still inactive.
claims.wrongResult: The newly held panel is wrapped in `<Activity mode="visible">` and stays there indefinitely: it keeps its effects mounted and is never put at `display: none`, instead of resting in the hidden Activity the policy promises for an inactive panel.
claims.contract: `MountHold.hidden` TSDoc: "Whether the held panel is resting — the `<Activity mode=\"hidden\">` state." `useMountHold` remark: "Either way a panel mounting inactive starts hidden, so a held panel never pays a visible first render it doesn't need." `Hold` remark: "A hidden Activity keeps its subtree in the DOM at `display: none` with state intact, tears its effects down, and defers its re-renders off the visible commit."
claims.evidence: The rest latch is seeded once: `const [rested, setRested] = useState(!active && held && defer)` at line 99, evaluated only on the first render. The render-time correction at line 104 — `if (rested && (active || !held || !defer)) setRested(false)` — is one-directional; it clears the latch but never sets it. `held` is derived per render at line 95 (`mount !== 'active'`) and `defer` at line 84, so both can turn on after mount, and when they do `rested` is still `false` and `hidden: defer ? rested : !active` (line 116) reads `false`. `Hold` (hold.tsx:32) then renders `<Activity mode="visible">`. The only writer is `rest` (lines 109-111), which `CurrentContent` calls solely from a landed fade-out (current-content.tsx:156-163) — an animation that does not run for a panel mounting with `initial`/`animate` already at `{ opacity: 0 }` (current-content.tsx:147, :151). Suspected severity: low — narrow trigger (a runtime `mount` change), but it violates the stated `hidden` contract and leaves effects alive. Fix idea: add the symmetric render-time set, tracking the previous `held`/`defer` pair and latching `setRested(true)` when a hold turns on for an inactive panel, mirroring the mount-time seed.

claims.trigger: A consumer reads the public API and dismisses a batch in callback position: `const { dismiss } = useToast(); staleIds.forEach(dismiss)`.
claims.wrongResult: Each toast's `onDismiss` is invoked with the array index (`0`, `1`, `2`, …) as its dismiss reason instead of `'dismissed'`, so a consumer switching on `ToastDismissReason` matches no case and the closed reason set the API advertises is broken from outside.
claims.contract: `ToastContextValue.dismiss` TSDoc (providers/toast/context.ts): "Takes no reason, deliberately. The same closure sits on the viewport context, which does take one, but the reason vocabulary belongs to the provider: an application dismissal is `'dismissed'` by definition, and letting a caller claim `'timeout'` or `'evicted'` would turn a closed set into an open one." `ToastData.onDismiss` TSDoc (types.ts): "Fires once when this toast leaves the queue, with the reason it left."
claims.evidence: `ToastContextValue.dismiss` is declared `(id: string) => void` at providers/toast/context.ts:14, but the provider hands the two-argument implementation straight through: `dismiss` is defined at toast.tsx:62-92 as `(id: string, reason: ToastDismissReason = 'dismissed') => …` and placed on the public value unwrapped at toast.tsx:135 (`useMemo<ToastContextValue>(() => ({ toast, dismiss }), [toast, dismiss])`). A wider function is assignable to the narrower type, so the extra parameter survives; the default at line 63 only fires for `undefined`, and `Array.prototype.forEach` supplies `(value, index, array)`. The reason then flows unvalidated to the consumer at toast.tsx:87 (`toast.onDismiss?.(reason)`). The very same closure is deliberately re-exposed with its reason on the viewport value at toast.tsx:141, which is the shape the doccomment says the public API must not have. Suspected severity: low. Fix idea: publish a narrowed wrapper — `const publicDismiss = useCallback((id: string) => dismiss(id), [dismiss])` — and put that on `ToastContext`, keeping the two-argument form for `ToastViewportContext`.

claims.trigger: Hover a control that shows a tooltip, then open a deliberately non-modal overlay — for example `<Overlay modal={false} backdrop open>` (the shape `SidebarLayout`'s hover-revealed floating `Sheet` uses).
claims.wrongResult: The open tooltip is dismissed by the overlay signal even though no modal surface took over the page, so a pointer affordance that is documented as non-disclosing tears down unrelated non-modal floats.
claims.contract: `notifyOverlaySignal` TSDoc (primitives/overlay/overlay-signal.ts): "Broadcasts an overlay-lifecycle signal. Modal-style surfaces (dialog, sheet, drawer, popover) fire it on open; non-modal floats such as tooltips subscribe and close on any signal." `Overlay`'s own `modal` TSDoc: "Pass `false` for transient, pointer-driven surfaces (e.g. a hover-revealed sheet) that must not steal focus or block the page … the page behind stays interactive".
claims.evidence: The signal is fired unconditionally on the open edge with no modality guard: overlay.tsx:142-144 `useEffect(() => { if (open) notifyOverlaySignal() }, [open])`, sitting below the `modal = true` default at line 112 and the `!modal && 'pointer-events-none'` branch at line 150 that the rest of the component uses to distinguish the two arms. `notifyOverlaySignal` walks every subscriber (overlay-signal.ts:12-14), and the subscription doc at :16-23 names tooltips as the readers that "close when a modal surface takes over". packages/ui/src/layouts/sidebar/sidebar.tsx:105-123 is a live non-modal caller (`<Sheet … modal={false} backdrop>` driven by `onPointerEnter`), whose own TSDoc at sidebar.tsx:45-47 calls the peek "a pointer affordance rather than a disclosure". Suspected severity: low. Fix idea: gate the effect on modality — `if (open && modal) notifyOverlaySignal()` — or add an explicit `signal` prop so a caller that genuinely wants the takeover semantics can opt in.

claims.trigger: Wrap the shell in a split density scope that tightens spacing without shrinking type — `<Density space="sm" size="lg"><SidebarLayout sidebar={…}>…</SidebarLayout></Density>`.
claims.wrongResult: Every padding the layout owns grows instead of shrinking: the mobile navbar renders at the largest padding step, the content column keeps the largest horizontal and bottom padding, and the header keeps the largest vertical padding — the opposite of the requested `space="sm"`, which the layout ignores entirely.
claims.contract: `DensityToken` TSDoc (primitives/density/density.tsx): "Two axes, both keyed on {@link Step}: `space` controls padding + gap (the breathing-room dimension); `size` controls text + icon (the visual-heft dimension). The axes inherit independently. `<Density space="sm">` shrinks spacing without touching font size". `SidebarLayout` remark: "Sizes its padding and panel from ambient Density."
claims.evidence: sidebar.tsx:82 destructures only the heft axis — `const { size } = useDensity()` — and then feeds it to every spacing recipe: the navbar padding lookup `NAVBAR_PADDING[size]` at line 158 (the constant at line 32 is literally documented "Mobile navbar padding per Density step" and maps `sm: 'p-4', md: 'p-6', lg: 'p-8'`), the panel width `k.panel({ size })` at line 100, the content box `k.content({ size, stickyHeader })` at line 173, and the header `k.header({ size })` at line 190. In packages/ui/src/layouts/sidebar/variants.ts the `content` size variants are pure padding (lines 62-64: `px-4 pb-4 …pt-4` / `px-6 pb-6 …pt-6` / `px-8 pb-8 …pt-8`) and the `header` size variants likewise (lines 82-86: `lg:pt-4 pb-4` / `lg:pt-6 pb-6` / `lg:pt-8 pb-8`). The `space` axis is never read anywhere in the file, so the split token collapses to whichever `size` was set. The in-package precedent for the correct read is `ControlFrame` (primitives/control/control.tsx:21), which takes `const { space } = useDensity()` for its spacing-derived radius. Suspected severity: low-medium — silent on the diagonal presets, wrong whenever the two axes are split, which the token's doc names as its reason to exist. Fix idea: read both axes (`const { space, size } = useDensity()`) and key `NAVBAR_PADDING`, `k.content`, and `k.header` off `space` while leaving `k.panel` on whichever axis the rail width is meant to follow.

leads.note: `Stack` spreads `{...props}` after `direction="col"`, so the column is only a default; its own TSDoc records the unresolved contract in a public doccomment ("Unresolved by design, pending a maintainer call: Flex's own doc says 'use Flex for rows, Stack for columns', while `direction` here stays overridable and eight demos pass `direction="row"`"). `DashboardLayout` consumes it as if it laid out a row.

`scrollToIndex: virtualizer.scrollToIndex` is returned unwrapped (line 93) and the resync `useEffect` at lines 79-81 has no dependency array, so it runs after every commit. If the virtualizer re-binds `scrollToIndex` between renders, `VirtualOptions`' `source` memo (virtual-options.tsx:144-154) invalidates each render and its registration effect (:158-166) tears down and re-writes `registryRef.current` on every commit, briefly nulling the roving owner's item source.

The `--breakpoint-lg` auto-close subscribes inside a `useEffect` with `[]` deps (lines 35-49) and reads the token exactly once via `getComputedStyle(document.documentElement)`. A theme swap that changes the token leaves the listener bound to the stale media query, and the bail on an undefined token is permanent for the component's lifetime — both silently drop the auto-close that `SidebarLayout` and `DashboardLayout` document in their `onOpenChange` TSDoc.

`sharedProps` (`data-slot`, `data-variant`, `data-size`, `data-has-prefix`, `data-has-suffix`, `data-has-label`, lines 130-137) is written before `{...buttonProps}` / `{...props}` with the comment "consumer `props` spread later can still override". `data-has-label` and `data-size` are load-bearing wiring the button recipe keys its `data-[has-label]` selectors on, which CONVENTIONS §3.9 places after the spread.

claims.trigger: An element whose `aria-labelledby` holds the space-separated ID list ARIA permits, e.g. `<button aria-labelledby="lbl-verb lbl-noun">X</button>` with both target elements present in the document.
claims.wrongResult: The function returns the element's own text (`'X'`), not the text of the referenced labels. A keyboard-drag announcement therefore narrates the visible glyph of the handle instead of the card or column name the label elements carry, so the drag readout names the wrong object.
claims.contract: TSDoc on `accessibleName`: "Best-effort accessible name of a DOM element: its `aria-label`, the trimmed text of its `aria-labelledby` target, else its own trimmed text."
claims.evidence: Lines 14-18. `const labelledby = el.getAttribute('aria-labelledby')` returns the raw attribute string; `el.ownerDocument.getElementById(labelledby)` is then called with `'lbl-verb lbl-noun'`, which is not an element id, so `getElementById` returns `null`, `target?.textContent` is `undefined`, and the `??` falls through to `el.textContent`. The fallback is silent — there is no way for the caller to tell a resolved label from a fallback. Suspected severity: medium (a11y readout names the wrong object, and only for multi-IDREF labels, which is the exact case the label indirection exists to serve). Fix: split on `/\s+/`, map each token through `getElementById`, filter nullish, join the trimmed `textContent` values with a space, and fall back to `el.textContent` only when the join is empty.

claims.trigger: Call `announce('Copied')`, then have anything clear or replace `document.body`'s children (a test teardown that sets `document.body.innerHTML = ''`, a full-page swap, a portal root remount), then call `announce('Saved')`.
claims.wrongResult: The second call writes to a live region that is no longer in the document, so no screen reader announcement is made and the caller gets no error. Every later `announce` for that politeness level is silently dropped for the rest of the process.
claims.contract: TSDoc on `announce`: "Sends `message` to a visually-hidden `aria-live` region appended to `document.body`, lazily created on first use and shared process-wide."
claims.evidence: Lines 12-14 hold `politeRegion` / `assertiveRegion` in module scope; lines 32-42 `region(assertive)` uses `??=`, so it re-creates only when the cached value is `null`, never when the cached node is detached; line 55 `const node = region(assertive)` then lines 59-63 write `textContent` on that detached node. `__resetAnnouncer` (lines 67-73) is the only thing that nulls the cache, and it is test-only and not on the `core/index.ts` barrel, so production code has no route back. Suspected severity: medium (silent a11y loss, no throw, no console output). Fix: in `region()`, treat a cached node whose `isConnected` is false as absent — `if (!politeRegion?.isConnected) politeRegion = createRegion(false)`.

claims.trigger: Call `announce('Copied')`, wait for the announcement, then call `announce('Copied')` again with the identical string (a user pressing a copy button twice).
claims.wrongResult: The second identical message is not announced. The clear and the re-set both land inside one task, so the accessibility tree never observes a content change on the live region and the screen reader stays silent — exactly the repeat case the clear-then-set dance exists to cover.
claims.contract: Comment on the clear/set pair in `announce`: "Clears, then sets on the next microtask; live regions announce only observed mutations, even for identical messages."
claims.evidence: Lines 59-63: `node.textContent = ''` runs synchronously, then `queueMicrotask(() => { node.textContent = message })`. A microtask runs before the next rendering opportunity, i.e. before the accessibility tree is recomputed, so the net observed DOM state across the update-the-rendering step is unchanged from the previous message. Only a separation across a task boundary (`setTimeout(…, 0)`) or a frame (double `requestAnimationFrame`) makes the empty state observable to the AT. Suspected severity: medium (silent a11y loss on repeats; the first announcement of a *new* message still works, which is why it reads as working). Fix: replace `queueMicrotask` with a `setTimeout(…, 0)` (or a rAF pair) so the empty state survives one rendering opportunity.

claims.trigger: Two nested elements both wire a handler through `composeEventHandlers`. The inner element's library handler calls `event.preventDefault()` (a menu item swallowing Enter, say); the outer element's caller handler does nothing. The user presses the key on the inner element and the React synthetic event bubbles to the outer handler.
claims.wrongResult: The outer element's library handler never runs, even though the outer caller's handler never called `preventDefault`. The outer behaviour (roving move, dismiss, submit-suppression) is silently skipped, and the caller has no way to opt back in short of setting `checkForDefaultPrevented: false` and losing the guard entirely.
claims.contract: TSDoc on `composeEventHandlers`: "returns a single handler that runs `theirs` first, then `ours` — skipping `ours` when `theirs` called `event.preventDefault()`, unless `checkForDefaultPrevented` is `false`."
claims.evidence: Lines 36-40. The guard is `if (!checkForDefaultPrevented || !event.defaultPrevented) ours(event)`, read *after* `theirs?.(event)`. `event.defaultPrevented` is a property of the event, not of `theirs`: React reuses one `SyntheticEvent` instance for the whole bubble path, so any earlier handler anywhere on the path — a descendant's `ours`, an ancestor capture handler, a native listener — sets it. The documented condition is "`theirs` called `preventDefault`", which requires a before/after comparison. Suspected severity: medium (behaviour silently drops in exactly the nested-composition case the library is built out of; no error surfaces). Fix: snapshot `const wasPrevented = event.defaultPrevented` before `theirs?.(event)` and gate on `!checkForDefaultPrevented || wasPrevented || !event.defaultPrevented`.

claims.trigger: A kata that declares a slot and an extra of the same name, e.g. `defineRecipe({ slots: { title: 'text-lg font-semibold' } }, { title: someMotionBundle })`.
claims.wrongResult: No error is thrown and `k.title` silently resolves to the extra instead of the slot's merged class string, so every consumer that spreads `className={k.title}` gets an object rendered into the class attribute. The documented collision guard reports nothing.
claims.contract: TSDoc `@throws` on `defineRecipe`: "If a slot name collides with a recipe property — a function built-in (`name`, `length`, `call`, …) or the engine-attached `config` / `skeleton`."
claims.evidence: Lines 144-159. The guard at line 148 is `if (slot in recipe || slot === 'config' || slot === 'skeleton')`, evaluated before any assignment, so at that moment `recipe` carries only `Function.prototype` members. `Object.assign(recipe, slotCache)` runs at line 155, `Object.assign(recipe, extras)` at line 159 — extras are applied last and overwrite the slot properties with no check. `skeleton` and `config` are special-cased by name because they are attached after the loop; extras are the third such source and were missed. Suspected severity: low-medium (kata-authoring footgun that fails at render, not at definition). Fix: after the slot loop, check `extras` keys against `slotCache` (and against `'config'`) and throw with the same message shape.

claims.trigger: A kata declares a compound rule whose condition value is an array or object rather than a scalar, e.g. `compound: [{ size: ['sm', 'md'], class: 'gap-xs' }]`. The `CompoundRule` type accepts it because condition values are typed `string | ClassValue`, and `ClassValue` admits arrays and dictionaries.
claims.wrongResult: The rule never matches any call. `size: ['sm','md']` is coerced to the key `'sm,md'`, which no axis value can equal, so `gap-xs` is never emitted for either size. Nothing throws and `recipe.config.compound` shows the rule present, so the kata author sees a declared rule that produces no class.
claims.contract: TSDoc on `CompoundRule` (`core/recipe/engine/types.ts`): "A compound rule applies a class set when every named axis matches. The engine coerces a condition value to its axis key, the same conversion a caller's prop takes, so a rule on a `true` / `false` axis accepts `{ interactive: true }` and `{ interactive: 'true' }` alike."
claims.evidence: `types.ts` line 25 types the rule as `Record<string, string | ClassValue> & { class: ClassValue }`, so array and object condition values type-check. `recipe.ts` lines 186-191 `normalizeRule` sends every non-`class` entry through `axisKey`; `axisKey` (lines 175-177) is `String(value)`, which turns `['sm','md']` into `'sm,md'` and `{a:1}` into `'[object Object]'`. `matches` (lines 243-245) then compares that against `values[key]`, which only ever holds a real axis key, so the rule is dead. The mechanism is the unconditional `String()` coercion in this file; `types.ts` only supplies the permissive type. Suspected severity: low-medium (silent styling loss, discoverable only by inspecting rendered classes). Fix: narrow the condition value type to `string | number | boolean | null | undefined` in `CompoundRule`, or have `normalizeRule` throw when a condition value is a non-primitive.

claims.trigger: Any caller that mutates the returned object before spreading, e.g. `const attrs = validationAttrs('warning'); Object.assign(attrs, { 'data-warning': 'x' })` — or any library code that spreads it into a target and later writes back through the same reference.
claims.wrongResult: The mutation persists in the module-level singleton and every later `validationAttrs('warning')` anywhere in the app returns the mutated pair, so unrelated controls render the corrupted attribute. Nothing throws, contrary to the documented frozen guarantee.
claims.contract: TSDoc on `validationAttrs`: "Returns frozen singletons, so spreads stay referentially stable across renders."
claims.evidence: Lines 1 (`core/invalid-attrs.ts` `const INVALID = { … } as const`), 6 (`const WARNING = { 'data-warning': '' } as const`), 8 (`const VALID = { 'data-valid': '' } as const`), and 13-17 (`ATTRS`). `as const` is a type-level assertion only — it produces `readonly` property types for the compiler and performs no runtime `Object.freeze`. The objects are genuinely singletons (the referential-stability half of the sentence holds), but they are writable, so the "frozen" half is false and a stray write escapes the caller. Suspected severity: low (needs a misbehaving caller, but the blast radius is process-wide). Fix: wrap `INVALID`, `WARNING`, and `VALID` in `Object.freeze(...)`, or drop "frozen" from the doccomment.

claims.trigger: A focus-trap or roving container whose subtree contains a hidden input — `<form><input type="hidden" name="csrf" value="…" /><button>Save</button></form>` inside a dialog — then querying the subtree with `FOCUSABLE_SELECTOR` and focusing the first match.
claims.wrongResult: The hidden input is returned as the first focusable descendant. `HTMLElement.focus()` on it is a no-op, so focus stays where it was — outside the trap for an opening dialog — and the keyboard user is left stranded outside the surface. The same false positive shifts every index in a roving list, so arrow keys land one item off.
claims.contract: TSDoc on `FOCUSABLE_SELECTOR`: "Selector for the descendants in the tab order: links with an `href`, enabled form controls, and any element whose `tabindex` is not `-1`."
claims.evidence: Lines 10-11. The `input:not([disabled])` term matches every input element that carries no `disabled` attribute, including `type="hidden"`; a hidden input is never in the tab order and is not focusable. The @remarks block deliberately reasons about the `disabled` attribute versus `:disabled` but says nothing about `type`, so the omission looks like an oversight rather than a stated limit. Suspected severity: medium (WCAG 2.4.3 focus-order failure, and it reproduces on any form that ships a CSRF or state input). Fix: change the term to `input:not([disabled]):not([type="hidden"])`.

claims.trigger: Call `memoWeak(cache, key, compute)` twice with the same `key` where `compute` legitimately returns `undefined` — for example a per-node memo of "the nearest scrollable ancestor", which is `undefined` for a node that has none.
claims.wrongResult: The second call re-runs `compute` instead of returning the stored value. The memo never takes effect for that key, so a per-object cache degrades to an uncached call on exactly the inputs that answer "nothing here", and any side effect or DOM walk inside `compute` repeats on every read.
claims.contract: TSDoc on `memoWeak`: "The value under `key` in a {@link WeakMap}, computed and stored on the first read." and "@returns The cached value, computing it first when absent."
claims.evidence: Lines 15-17: `const hit = cache.get(key); if (hit !== undefined) return hit`. `WeakMap.get` returns `undefined` both for a missing key and for a key whose stored value is `undefined`, and the code cannot tell them apart. Line 21 does `cache.set(key, computed)` so the entry exists — the guard just never sees it. Contrast `once` in the same directory (`utilities/once.ts` lines 10-22), which keeps a separate `computed` boolean precisely to survive an `undefined` result, so the package already has the right shape one file over. Suspected severity: low (perf and repeated side effects, not a wrong value). Fix: gate on `cache.has(key)` and read with a non-null assertion, or keep the `get` fast path and fall back to `has` before recomputing.

claims.trigger: `const f = once(() => { throw new Error('boom') })`, then call `f()` twice inside a try/catch.
claims.wrongResult: `compute` runs a second time. Any caller that relies on the at-most-once guarantee for a side-effecting or expensive thunk — the deferred chart derivations the doccomment names — pays for it again on every retry after a transient failure, and a thunk that mutates external state applies its mutation twice.
claims.contract: TSDoc on `once`: "Wraps `compute` so it runs at most once, every later call returning the first result."
claims.evidence: Lines 14-22. `computed = true` is set on line 18, *after* `value = compute()` on line 16, so a throw leaves `computed === false` and the next call re-enters the branch. Whether retry-on-throw is desirable is arguable, but the doccomment states an unconditional at-most-once contract with no caveat. Suspected severity: low. Fix: either set `computed = true` before invoking `compute` (retaining the throw), or add an `@remarks` sentence stating that a throwing compute is retried.

claims.trigger: A press near the inline-start edge of a bordered, vertically scrolling element under `direction: rtl` — e.g. `<div dir="rtl" style="border: 2px solid; overflow-y: auto">` with the pointer a couple of pixels inside the content, so `offsetX` is at or below the border width plus the scrollbar width.
claims.wrongResult: A press on real content is reported as a scrollbar press. The floating surface above it does not dismiss and a drag selection is not put down, so an RTL user cannot close a popover by clicking near the start edge of a bordered scroller.
claims.contract: TSDoc on `isScrollbarPress`: "@returns True when the point sits in the vertical or the horizontal gutter" and "@remarks An axis is only tested where it can actually scroll, so a bordered box that does not overflow has no gutter to press."
claims.evidence: Lines 39-41: the RTL branch is `event.offsetX <= target.offsetWidth - target.clientWidth`. `offsetX` is measured from the *padding* edge (CSSOM View), while `offsetWidth - clientWidth` is the scrollbar width **plus** `borderLeftWidth + borderRightWidth`, so the threshold overshoots the gutter by the two border widths. The LTR branch on line 41 (`event.offsetX > target.clientWidth`) is correct precisely because `clientWidth` already excludes borders — the two branches are measured against different origins. The `<=` versus `>` asymmetry also makes `offsetX === 0` a hit in RTL while the matching LTR edge pixel is a miss. Suspected severity: low-medium (RTL-only, needs a bordered scroller, but silently defeats dismissal). Fix: compute the gutter as `target.offsetWidth - target.clientWidth - Number.parseFloat(style.borderInlineStartWidth) - Number.parseFloat(style.borderInlineEndWidth)` and test `event.offsetX < gutter`.

claims.trigger: `keyByOccurrence(['a', 'a', 'a�1'])` — a duplicated value alongside a value that literally contains the NUL separator plus an index.
claims.wrongResult: The returned keys are `['a', 'a�1', 'a�1']`: the synthesised key for the second `'a'` collides with the pass-through key for the third entry. React logs "Encountered two children with the same key", and the reconciler drops or reorders one of the two rows on the next update — the exact duplicate-key failure the helper exists to prevent.
claims.contract: TSDoc on `keyByOccurrence`: "Pair each string with a React-key-safe identifier: the value itself for the first occurrence, suffixed with its occurrence index for repeats. Lists with duplicates (controlled tag values, un-deduped validation messages) collide on bare value keys."
claims.evidence: Line 15: `key: occurrence === 0 ? value : `${value}�${occurrence}``. The escape uses an in-band separator over an alphabet (arbitrary user strings — tag values, validation messages) that is not guaranteed to exclude it, so the mapping is not injective. Suspected severity: low (needs a NUL in caller data, but the input is untrusted tag/message text). Fix: make the key injective by always suffixing — `${occurrence}�${value}` — so the index prefix is unambiguous, or escape any existing `�` in `value` before appending.

claims.trigger: `resolveFormat({ type: 'id', prefix: 'INV', pad: 4 })(Number.NaN)`, or the same formatter applied to `Number.POSITIVE_INFINITY` — a grid cell whose id column holds a missing or overflowed number.
claims.wrongResult: Renders `'INV-00NaN'` and `'INV-Infinity'`. The documented behaviour is that non-finite values come out as `Intl` renders them (`NaN`, `∞`), so a caller that guards on the documented glyphs sees a zero-padded `00NaN` string in the cell instead.
claims.contract: TSDoc @remarks on `resolveFormat`: "Non-finite values format as `Intl` renders them (`NaN`, `∞`); a caller that wants a gap glyph guards before calling."
claims.evidence: Line 144 short-circuits the `id` spec to `formatId` before any `Intl.NumberFormat` is built, so the remark's premise does not hold for that branch. `formatId` (lines 118-128): `Math.trunc(NaN)` is `NaN`, `Math.abs(NaN).toString()` is `'NaN'`, and `digits.padStart(4, '0')` yields `'00NaN'`; `Math.abs(Infinity).toString()` is `'Infinity'`, which `padStart(4)` leaves alone. Suspected severity: low (cosmetic, but the remark is the only guidance a caller has for the non-finite case, and it is wrong for one of the two spec kinds). Fix: guard `formatId` with `Number.isFinite(value)` and route non-finite values through the numeric formatter, or scope the remark to numeric specs and document the `id` behaviour separately.

claims.trigger: Call `printInHiddenFrame({ prepare })` with no `onFail` inside `try { … } catch (error) { showToast(error) }`, in a context where the browser blocks `window.print()` (a sandboxed iframe, a pop-up-blocked print, a cross-origin `src` that makes `win.addEventListener` throw `SecurityError`).
claims.wrongResult: The caller's `catch` never runs. The error is thrown from inside the iframe's `load` listener, long after `printInHiddenFrame` returned, so it surfaces only as an uncaught window error — the caller gets neither a toast nor any signal, which is the silence the `onFail` doc says omitting the callback avoids.
claims.contract: TSDoc on the `onFail` option: "Omit it where the caller has nothing to fall back to, and a blocked `print()` propagates instead of going silent."
claims.evidence: Lines 60-80: the try/catch sits inside the `iframe.addEventListener('load', …)` callback; line 76 `if (!onFail) throw error` rethrows on the event-loop task that dispatched `load`. `printInHiddenFrame` itself returns synchronously at line 90 after `document.body.appendChild(iframe)`, so there is no synchronous frame for the caller's `try` to catch. "Propagates" is true only in the sense of reaching `window.onerror`. Suspected severity: low-medium (the failure route the doc singles out as observable is the one route the caller cannot observe). Fix: return a `Promise<void>` from `printInHiddenFrame` that rejects on the failure routes, or reword the option doc to say the throw reaches the global error handler, not the caller.

claims.trigger: Any caller passing a `slot` or `attr` argument that contains a CSS-significant character — `querySlot(container, 'menu"item', 'row-id', id)` or an `attr` built from a data key such as `'col.name'`.
claims.wrongResult: `querySelector` throws a `DOMException: Failed to execute 'querySelector' … is not a valid selector` instead of returning `HTMLElement | null`, so a keyboard-reorder hook that calls it inside a post-update effect crashes the render pass rather than degrading to "item not found".
claims.contract: TSDoc on `querySlot`: "Locates the element stamped `data-slot="<slot>"` whose `data-<attr>` equals `id`, scoped to `container` … Keyboard-reorder hooks use it to re-find an item by a stable id after a state update re-renders the DOM." The declared return type is `HTMLElement | null`.
claims.evidence: Lines 13-17. Only `id` is escaped: `[data-slot="${slot}"][data-${attr}="${CSS.escape(id)}"]`. `slot` is interpolated raw inside the quoted attribute value and `attr` raw into the attribute *name* position, where a dot, bracket, or quote terminates the selector. The escape on `id` shows the hazard was recognised for one of the three interpolations. Suspected severity: low (both arguments are library-supplied at today's call sites, but `querySlot` is a public `ui/core` export and the signature invites arbitrary strings). Fix: run `slot` through `CSS.escape` too and `attr` through `CSS.escape` in identifier position, or narrow the parameter types to a literal union of the slot/attr names the package actually stamps.

leads.note: The `barrelExports` scanner uses `/export\s*\{([^}]*)\}/g`, which does not match `export type { … } from './x'` because `type` sits between `export` and the brace. Every type-only re-export in a barrel is therefore invisible to the check, so an `@internal` *type* on a barrel passes the gate. `packages/ui/src/types/index.ts` is composed almost entirely of `export type { … }` lines and is effectively unscanned.

groups.cause: DatePickerSingle's `input` branch (date-picker.tsx:307-347) hands DateInput an incomplete prop set: it pins `format` to a literal that overrides the locale resolution DateInput would perform, and it never forwards the `invalid` the hook already resolved.

Across all three DatePicker state hooks, `readOnly` is spent on the `setOpen` callback alone: no value writer (`handleClear`, `handleSelect`, `togglePreset`, `applyDraft`) reads it, the trigger's clear button has no readOnly term, the input branch never forwards it, and a caller-controlled `open` bypasses even the open gate because `useControllable` returns the prop verbatim.

The relative variant identifies a committed span only by re-resolving it to a preset, so two spans that resolve equal collapse onto one preset: the highlight loses a row and cannot toggle it off, and the chip list emits one key and one label twice.

openQuestions.question: Q1 — Under `readOnly`, does the trigger's clear affordance disappear, or stay rendered and inert?
openQuestions.axes: Parity against the sibling the trigger cites: date-input.tsx:325 `if (!clearable || !hasValue || disabled || readOnly) return resolved` already hides it, and date-picker-trigger.tsx:96-98 declares the Listbox/Combobox mirror. Against that, the trigger's clear returns focus to the trigger as it unmounts (:162 `triggerButtonRef.current?.focus()`), so hiding it changes the focus story for a control readOnly deliberately keeps focusable.
openQuestions.changes: Hide: the gate lands in `DatePickerTrigger.showClear` (a new `readOnly` prop) and the two families agree, so S2 keeps date-picker-trigger.tsx in its file set. Inert: the gate lands only in the hooks' `handleClear`, S2 drops date-picker-trigger.tsx, and a button that looks actionable and does nothing becomes the accepted behaviour.

openQuestions.question: Q2 — Does `DatePicker`'s `format` keep its pinned `'MM/DD/YYYY'` default, or defer to the ambient locale as DateInput and the picker's own trigger label already do?
openQuestions.axes: date-picker.tsx:42 `@defaultValue 'MM/DD/YYYY'` is an accurate public annotation, and the 2026-09-12 doc audit ruled every `@defaultValue` accurate — so changing the behaviour changes a published default. Against it: date-input.tsx:117-118 names the DatePicker pairing as the reason the locale default exists, use-date-picker-state.ts:272 already reads the ambient locale for the trigger label, and packages/ui/REFERENCE.md:37 records that `locale needs an API decision — explicit props or app wrappers — because formats cannot move to CSS.`
openQuestions.changes: Defer: S3 drops the destructure default and the typed field agrees with the calendar and the trigger label under any locale; the annotation on that prop stops describing the code. Keep: B01-C01 becomes a documentation conflict rather than a behavioural fix, S3 narrows to the `invalid` forward, and only the relative Start/End fields need a locale-derived format so the custom range agrees with the calendar beside it.

openQuestions.question: Q3 — May the relative value hold two spans that resolve equal, or must a commit dedupe them?
openQuestions.axes: date-picker-relative-utilities.ts:238-239 says multi-select `rebuilds the result in preset order so chips stay stable and deduped`, which reads against holding one span per picked preset; but the value is consumed as an opaque span list by apps/places (places-filter.ts:24 `visited?: DatePickerRelativeValue[]`, :65-67 `ranges.some(…)`), where a duplicate span is harmless and a shape change is not. The URL round-trip at places-url.ts:72 can also hydrate a duplicate with no picks behind it.
openQuestions.changes: Dedupe on commit: the value stays `DatePickerRelativeValue[]`, S4 confines itself to deriving the highlight from `pickedIds` rather than from the spans, and two colliding rows both read pressed while the trigger shows one chip. Keep one entry per pick: each entry needs a preset id, so the array element type changes and S4 reaches apps/places' imports and its URL codec.

ruledOut.id: B01-C09 — the dropped part: "when the stepped year falls outside the visible decade no cell is marked at all and focus drops to the grid's first cell"

groups.cause: CONVENTIONS.md §3.9 is inverted in three wrappers: the load-bearing attribute is written before `{...props}`, so a consumer key of the same name wins — the §7.2 cascade wiring on Checkbox (`defaultChecked` reaching the same input as the bound `checked`) and the hard-coded `role` on RadioGroup and CheckboxGroup.

RangeSlider takes the `name` binding but not the rest of the control cascade its single-thumb sibling Slider completes: it destructures only `value`/`setValue` from `useFormValue`, so `setTouched` is never called and `invalid` never reaches `invalidAttrs`.

`useRangePointer`'s `onPointerDown` diverges from `useColorDrag`, the model its own comment names: it calls `preventDefault()` without the compensating synchronous focus, and it guards on `disabled` without the `event.button !== 0` test.

A presentational sub-part rendered with `<Input>` self-resolves the enclosing `<Field>`'s Control context and adopts field-level attributes that belong to the real control — FileUpload's readonly display box takes the field id and `required`, and each ColorPanel channel input takes `required` and `aria-describedby`.

groups.cause: Resolved structural wiring is written before `{...props}`, so a consumer prop overwrites the component's own `type`, widget ARIA state, derived ids, or roving handler — the inverse of CONVENTIONS.md:43 §3.9, whose stated precedent (`menu-item.tsx`) and whose sibling implementations (`tab.tsx:176-193`, `sidebar.tsx:78-81`) already do it the right way round.

The anchor branch of a polymorphic item omits a guard its own button branch carries: MenuItem's link row gets no `onKeyDown`, so Space is dead where the button row activates; CommandPaletteItem's disabled link keeps its `href`, so the auxiliary pointer paths navigate where MenuItem's disabled link degrades to a `<span>`.

openQuestions.question: Q1 — In the §3.9 reorder, does `data-slot` move after `{...props}` with the rest of the wiring, or stay overridable?
openQuestions.axes: CONVENTIONS.md:43 says both things: load-bearing structural attributes go after the spread, and `a leaf's \`data-slot\` default is destructured so a consumer can rename the anchor`. For `SidebarItem` the anchor is load-bearing — `sidebar.tsx:46 itemSelector: '[data-slot="sidebar-item-inner"]:not(:disabled)'` — so renaming it drops the row out of roving (B04-C08). The axes are: is `data-slot` presentational (renameable) or structural once a roving selector keys on it, and is the answer per-component or package-wide?
openQuestions.changes: Structural: S1 moves `data-slot` after the spread in `nav-item.tsx` and `sidebar-item.tsx`, and the C08 `data-slot` arm closes with the rest. Presentational: `data-slot` stays where it is, the C08 `data-slot` arm moves to the ruled-out list with §3.9's second half as its guard, and Sidebar's roving needs a selector that does not depend on a renameable anchor.

openQuestions.question: Q2 — For `TabList`, in what order do the roving handler and a consumer `onKeyDown` run, and does a consumer `preventDefault` suppress roving?
openQuestions.axes: `sidebar.tsx:78-81` runs roving first, then the consumer's. `menu-item-utilities.ts:37-43` runs the consumer's first and skips activation when the event is already `defaultPrevented`. The axes are: which handler owns the arrow keys, and whether a consumer can opt out of roving for a specific key.
openQuestions.changes: Roving-first (Sidebar precedent): S1's `tab-list.tsx` edit is a two-line compose and a consumer cannot suppress an arrow. Consumer-first with a `defaultPrevented` gate (MenuItem precedent): the compose needs the guard, and the new test must cover both the composed case and the suppressed case. Either way the two in-package precedents should stop disagreeing.

openQuestions.question: Q3 — How does an anchor branch express "disabled", and how does a link row answer Space?
openQuestions.axes: MenuItem removes the anchor entirely (`menu-item.tsx:68-82`, a `<span>` with `role="menuitem"`, `tabIndex={-1}`, `aria-disabled`); CommandPaletteItem keeps the anchor and guards only the click. For Space: APG says a menuitem activates on Enter and Space, but an anchor natively answers Enter only, so the row must either synthesise a click (which navigates and fires `onAction`) or `preventDefault` and call `onAction` directly (which does not navigate). The axes are: anchor-removal versus href-stripping, and click-synthesis versus direct activation for a link row.
openQuestions.changes: Anchor-removal: S2's palette edit mirrors MenuItem and the two components converge on one shape. Href-stripping: the palette keeps a focusable anchor with no destination, which needs its own reasoning about what the row then does on Enter. Click-synthesis on Space: the link navigates, matching a dropdown's current behaviour exactly (`use-a11y-roving.ts:617`). Direct activation: Space fires `onAction` and closes without navigating, which diverges from the dropdown and must be documented in MenuItem's TSDoc.

openQuestions.question: Q4 — Is `MenuContent`'s accessible name a static-menu-only prop, or a name for every mode?
openQuestions.axes: The prop's doccomments scope it to static menus (`menu-content.tsx:14`, `:17`) and the only test covers that path (`menu.test.tsx:195-206`), but a right-click menu has no trigger to borrow a name from either, and the type accepts the prop unconditionally on every mode. A dropdown is the one mode with a trigger, so it could take `aria-labelledby` pointed at the trigger instead of an author-supplied name. The axes are: which modes need an author-supplied name, and whether an accepted-but-ignored prop is acceptable on the modes that do not.
openQuestions.changes: Every-mode: S3 forwards both attributes on the floating branch and rewrites the two doccomments. Static-and-context only: S3 forwards on the context branch and gives the dropdown an automatic `aria-labelledby` off its trigger. Static-only: S3 becomes a type narrowing plus a doc note instead of a forward, and B04-C03 closes as a typing gap rather than an a11y gap.

openQuestions.question: Q5 — When a `SidebarItem` carries both an explicit `suffix` and a `SidebarItemActions` child, what renders?
openQuestions.axes: The doccomments promise "an explicit `suffix` wins" (`sidebar-item-actions.tsx:12-13`) and that the actions child "drops out of the inner content" (`sidebar-item.tsx:38-39`); together they delete the subtree, which neither doc states. The axes are: does the losing content fall back into the inner button (where `sidebar-item.tsx:90-92` warns an interactive control breaks the markup), take the slot anyway, render in a second slot, or become a development-time error?
openQuestions.changes: Inner fallback: S5 is a one-condition change in `resolveItemChildren` and the doc gains a sentence — but interactive controls then nest inside the `<button>`, which the file's own comment argues against. Actions-win: the doccomments invert and any consumer relying on "suffix wins" changes behaviour. Documented error: S5 becomes a dev warning plus a doc note and nothing renders differently in production.

openQuestions.question: Q6 — Does the document-position sort go into `queryItems` for every roving consumer, or only where the selector is a list?
openQuestions.axes: `queryItems` (`use-a11y-roving.ts:61-65`) is read by every consumer in this scope, and it runs on the arrow-key auto-repeat path — `resolveRovingContext` already skips it for indexed mode specifically to avoid "the DOM query (plus the array allocation) on every keystroke" (`:398-403`). Every other in-scope consumer passes a single-kind selector today (`tab-list.tsx:45`, `sidebar.tsx:46`, `stepper.tsx:122`, `popover.tsx:31`), so only Toolbar is exposed. The axes are: blast radius versus per-keystroke cost, and whether a jsdom-only artefact justifies a hook-wide change at all.
openQuestions.changes: Hook-wide: S6 is one edit in `queryItems`, every future list selector is safe, and the sort cost lands on every arrow press. Toolbar-only: S6 sorts at the Toolbar call site or flattens `TOOLBAR_ITEM_SELECTOR`, leaving the hook untouched and the next list-selector consumer exposed. No change: B04-C11 is accepted as a jsdom artefact and recorded as a test-authoring caveat instead.

openQuestions.question: Q7 — Does `Stepper` join the §7.3 `null` contract, or is an index-only root a documented exemption?
openQuestions.axes: CONVENTIONS.md:77 states the contract unconditionally, `useControllable` already implements both arms (`use-controllable.ts:9-10`), and the sibling `Current` root carries the `null` arm (`current.ts:37-38`). Against that: a step index is a value a flow always has, `onValueChange` currently coerces (`stepper.tsx:98 (next) => onValueChange?.(next ?? 0)`) so the public callback never emits `null`, and the 2026-07-13 audit recorded the whole axis as screened out before flagging. The axes are: contract uniformity versus the semantics of "a stepper with no current step", and whether widening the callback is a breaking change for existing owners.
openQuestions.changes: Joins: S7 widens `value` and `onValueChange`, drops the coercion, and must answer what a `null`-valued Stepper renders — no step marked current, no `aria-current="step"`, and what `StepperStep` computes for its state. Exempt: S7 shrinks to a doccomment on `stepper.tsx:16-17` naming the exemption, and B04-C13's remaining half closes as documented rather than fixed.

ruledOut.guard:
The cloned-child branch is not affected and is not part of the confirmed finding. packages/ui/src/components/menu/menu-trigger.tsx:113-131 `return cloneElement(child, {
			...getReferenceProps({` … `}),
			ref: mergeRefs,
			'aria-haspopup': 'menu',
			'aria-expanded': open,
			'aria-controls': open ? menuId : undefined,
			'data-slot': 'menu-trigger',` — the five attributes are written after the spread, so they win. Every consumer-root site takes this branch (see the C01 reach entry), which is why the claim's reach is NONE.

The worked example — "the second press lands on the trailing anchor instead of the adjacent button" — is not traced as stated, because under the same grouping the resting stop is itself mis-seated: packages/ui/src/hooks/a11y/use-a11y-roving.ts:350 `return bySelector ?? items[0]` puts the initial `tabIndex=0` on the first grouped match (the anchor), not on the DOM-first button, so "from the first control" does not start where the claim assumes. What traces is the general form: the item order is grouped by selector rather than by document position, and the resting stop follows that wrong order. The production arm is refuted outright — a spec-conforming `querySelectorAll` returns document order, so the defect exists only under jsdom/nwsapi, as the repository's own caveat at use-a11y-roving.ts:54-55 records.

leads: `packages/ui/src/modules/grid/grid-manager-color-menu.tsx:53` passes `aria-label={`Color menu for ${label}`}` to `Menu`, but `MenuProps` (packages/ui/src/components/menu/menu.tsx:15-42) declares no `aria-label` — the prop is either a JSX excess-property error or silently dropped on a `display: contents` wrapper. This is the call site the prior-art row `[SURFACED] \`Menu\` — it silently drops \`aria-label\` (a call site passes one today)` names. Adjacent to B04-C03; not judged.

`MenuTrigger`'s cloned-child branch writes only five attributes after `getReferenceProps` (packages/ui/src/components/menu/menu-trigger.tsx:126-129); a cloned child's own `type`, `role`, or `tabIndex` still reaches the DOM unchanged. Whether a cloned child's explicit prop should be honoured (the consumer chose the element) or overridden (the trigger owns the wiring) is a cross-component question the file alone does not settle — `TooltipTrigger` and `PopoverTrigger` are named in the same comment as the shared pattern.

`Button` destructures `type` (packages/ui/src/components/button/button.tsx:94) and re-emits it at :178 before `{...buttonProps}` at :180, so `type` can never be pinned by a caller that routes through `Button`: NavItem's and SidebarItem's `type="button"` is a default the consumer overrides no matter where the caller puts it in its own JSX. Any §3.9 fix for the nav/tab/sidebar family therefore depends on `Button`'s ordering, not the caller's — a cross-component seam wider than S1.

`packages/ui/src/components/stepper/stepper.tsx:98` `onValueChange: (next) => onValueChange?.(next ?? 0)` coerces a cleared value to `0` before the owner sees it, so the public callback can never report "no current step" even if the hook below it does. Adjacent to B04-C13; not judged.

`Stepper`'s interactivity gate (`stepper.tsx:104` `const interactive = onValueChange !== undefined || defaultValue !== undefined`) and `StepperStep`'s button/div branch (`stepper-step.tsx:123` `if (onValueChange !== undefined) {`) read two different things — the root's own prop versus the context value the root computes at `:137`. They agree today only because the root writes `interactive ? setCurrent : undefined`; the coupling is undocumented. Not judged.

`useA11yRoving`'s main item query is unsorted for every consumer (`use-a11y-roving.ts:61-65`, called at `:403` and `:891`) while `rowControls` sorts (`:46-58`). Only Toolbar passes a multi-kind selector today, so only Toolbar is exposed — but the next consumer to pass a selector list inherits the same jsdom ordering artefact with nothing to warn it. A cross-component seam behind B04-C11; the hook-wide question is Q6.

openQuestions.question: Q2 — Should KanbanColumnBody's emptiness test use React's own child walk or a hand-rolled filter over the raw array?
openQuestions.axes: The digest's reverted Stepper change shows `Children.toArray` drops false children and shifts stamped keys, which matters where children are keyed; here the body only counts, and it renders `children` verbatim.
openQuestions.changes: A hand-rolled filter keeps the render path untouched and the diff at one line. Adopting `Children.toArray` for the count re-opens the question the Stepper reversal settled, and would want a note against that precedent.

openQuestions.question: Q3 — Does the reorderable row's Tab stop follow `activates` (href or own onClick), or a real focusable-descendant probe?
openQuestions.axes: `activates` is a prop-time derivation and cannot see a focusable child, which is the shape the grid column manager ships (see leads); a probe needs DOM measurement and a render pass, and the ListItem @remarks promises exactly one stop per row either way.
openQuestions.changes: Following `activates` is a one-line change confined to list-item.tsx and closes the claim as written, leaving the focusable-child case open. A probe closes both but adds an effect and a measurement to every reorderable row, and would fold the lead into this scope.

openQuestions.question: Q4 — Should the read-only key fallback be the render position, or should the identity map stay?
openQuestions.axes: A positional key is what the TSDoc promises and fixes duplicate primitives, but it remounts rows when a read-only array reorders; the identity map is stable across reorders and fails only on duplicate values. The List type already confines the fallback to read-only lists, so the drag-remount warning in list.tsx:70-73 does not apply.
openQuestions.changes: Positional keys make S6 a two-line change in use-list-drag.ts. Keeping the map and instead deduplicating collided values keeps reorder stability but adds a counter and changes the emitted `data-item-id` shape.

openQuestions.question: Q5 — Does `stampTreePositions` descend into Fragments only, or into any non-element child container?
openQuestions.axes: Fragments are the documented React idiom for a conditional group and the claim's trigger; arrays already flatten. A general descent changes what "rendered siblings" means for wrapper components, which the TreePositionValue TSDoc defines as a level, not a DOM depth.
openQuestions.changes: Fragment-only keeps S7 inside tree-item-children.tsx and matches the quoted contract. A general descent would also have to define what a wrapper component contributes to `setsize`, which reaches tree-item-content.tsx and the context's documented meaning.

openQuestions.question: Q6 — Should the virtualized tree re-derive `defaultExpandDepth` when `data` identity changes, or converge on the recursive variant's per-render resolution?

openQuestions.question: Q7 — Does the no-op-change bail live in `expand`, or in `useControllable`?
openQuestions.axes: `expand` is local and closes only this row; `useControllable` is package-wide and would stop every controlled component from firing a callback with an identical value — a semantics change for every consumer of the hook, well outside this scope.

openQuestions.question: Q8 — Does JsonTree adopt the hook's index-based `itemSource`, or keep real roving focus and bound Home/End and the wrap to the true list?

groups.cause: One `<Button>` call in `hold-button.tsx` sits on the wrong side of its own spread in both directions at once: the load-bearing `type` is written before `{...props}` where §3.9 puts it after, and the presentational `data-slot` is written after where §3.9 asks for a destructured default — so a consumer can override the attribute that must not be overridden and cannot override the one that should be.

The sheet kata's shared bases were authored for a panel docked to a side, and the `top`/`bottom` arms were added without clearing them: the side-blind `width` scale keeps its `sm:max-w-*` cap on a panel meant to span the screen, and the handle area keeps its `absolute inset-y-0` full-height reach on a grip meant to be an edge strip. Both resolve in `recipes/kata/sheet.ts` and both surface only on `side="top"` or `side="bottom"`.
